q: Before beginning a 12-lead EKG on an inpatient, the technician must verify the patient's identity. Which action meets the standard?
choices: Ask the patient to confirm the room number posted on the door
Call the patient's name and proceed if someone answers
Ask the patient to state name and date of birth, then compare both to the armband and the order
Match the face to the photo the nurse described at the desk
why: Two patient identifiers must be patient-specific, such as full name and date of birth, verified against the armband and requisition. Room number is never an acceptable identifier because patients are moved between rooms.

q: A technician enters the room and immediately begins attaching limb electrodes without speaking. What essential step was omitted?
choices: Introducing himself by name and title and explaining what the EKG involves
Charting the skin condition
Calibrating the machine to 20 mm/mV
Measuring the patient's height
why: Introduction and a plain-language explanation are required before any contact; they establish rapport and support consent. Calibration is a machine step and is normally 10 mm/mV, not a substitute for patient communication.

q: A fully alert adult says he does not want the EKG done. The technician should:
choices: Perform it anyway because a physician ordered it
Tell him the hospital will bill him for refusing
Apply the electrodes but not record a tracing
Stop, respect the refusal, and notify the nurse or ordering provider and document it
why: A competent adult may refuse any procedure; the technician stops, reports the refusal up the chain, and documents it. Performing it over an objection would constitute battery, no matter who ordered it.

q: While placing precordial electrodes on a female patient, the best way to protect dignity is to:
choices: Leave the door open so a witness can see the procedure
Expose only the area needed at the moment and keep the chest draped otherwise
Ask the patient to remove the gown entirely for accuracy
Have another patient's family member stay in the room
why: Expose only what is necessary for correct placement and re-drape immediately; a sheet or towel over the chest preserves privacy without shifting electrodes. Complete exposure is unnecessary because V1 through V6 can be placed one at a time.

q: A 4-year-old is crying and pulling at the electrodes. The most effective approach is:
choices: Use simple words, allow the child to touch an electrode first, and let a caregiver stay nearby
Explain lead vectors so the child understands the science
Tell the child the test will hurt only a little
Restrain the arms and work quickly
why: Short, concrete explanation plus caregiver presence and a chance to handle the equipment reduces pediatric fear. Saying it will hurt is both inaccurate, since an EKG is painless, and damages trust.

q: An elderly patient with mild hearing loss keeps saying What? The technician should:
choices: Shout each instruction from the doorway
Write out every word of the procedure
Face the patient, speak slowly in a lower pitch, and reduce background noise
Use only gestures and skip verbal explanation
why: Facing the patient allows lip reading, and age-related loss affects high frequencies first, so lowering pitch helps more than volume. Shouting raises pitch and distorts speech, making comprehension worse.

q: A patient speaks only Vietnamese. Which action is correct?
choices: Ask the patient's teenage daughter to translate
Use a hospital-approved medical interpreter in person or by phone
Speak English loudly and slowly
Proceed without explanation since an EKG is noninvasive
why: A qualified medical interpreter ensures accurate understanding and is required for meaningful consent. Family members, especially minors, are not acceptable interpreters because of accuracy and confidentiality problems.

q: A patient with moderate dementia becomes agitated when the technician reaches for the chest. The best response is:
choices: Complete the tracing as fast as possible despite the agitation
Tell the patient the test is required by law
Ask the family to hold the patient's arms
Speak calmly, use one short instruction at a time, and re-approach after the patient settles
why: Simple one-step directions, a calm tone, and a pause reduce agitation in cognitive impairment. Physical restraint by family is not within the technician's authority and can escalate distress and cause injury.

q: Which is an example of an open-ended question?
choices: Do you have chest pain?
Is the pain sharp?
Can you tell me what you were feeling when the pain started?
Did it last more than five minutes?
why: Open-ended questions invite description and cannot be answered yes or no, yielding richer symptom detail. Asking whether pain is sharp is a closed question that limits the patient to confirming the examiner's wording.

q: A patient is visibly anxious before a 12-lead. The most therapeutic statement is:
choices: There is nothing to be nervous about
This test does not use any electricity, and it records your heartbeat painlessly. What worries you most?
Everyone gets nervous, just relax
I will be done in one minute if you hold still
why: Correcting the common fear of being shocked plus an invitation to voice concerns is factual reassurance combined with active listening. Telling a patient there is nothing to be nervous about dismisses the feeling and shuts down communication.

q: Which action is an unauthorized disclosure of PHI under HIPAA?
choices: Posting a de-identified looking rhythm strip on a personal social media account with the patient's room number in the caption
Handing the tracing to the ordering physician
Placing the tracing in the patient's chart
Discussing the tracing with the covering nurse at the bedside
why: Room number plus date and facility can re-identify a patient, and social media posting of any patient material is prohibited regardless of intent. Sharing with the treating physician or nurse is a permitted treatment disclosure.

q: The minimum necessary standard means:
choices: Only the physician may view a chart
Records must be kept for the minimum legal period
Access PHI only to the extent needed to perform your specific job duty
Only the minimum number of leads may be recorded
why: Minimum necessary limits use, access and disclosure of PHI to what the task requires; a technician looks up the order and demographics, not unrelated history. It is not a records retention rule, which is governed separately.

q: A visitor in the hallway overhears the technician asking a patient about chest pain through a partly open door. This is best described as:
choices: A reportable HIPAA breach requiring notification
An incidental disclosure, permissible if reasonable safeguards were used
Negligence requiring an incident report
A violation of the minimum necessary rule
why: Incidental disclosures that occur despite reasonable safeguards, such as lowering the voice and closing the door, are permitted by HIPAA. A reportable breach involves unsecured PHI disclosed in a way not permitted by the rule.

q: A completed EKG tracing left face up on an unattended counter in a hallway is a problem because:
choices: The paper may curl and distort the waveform
It will lose thermal contrast
It cannot be scanned later
It contains PHI, including name and date of birth, visible to passersby
why: The demographic header makes the tracing protected health information that must be secured. Paper curling affects readability but is not the privacy issue the question targets.

q: A patient's chart contains a valid advance directive naming a health care proxy. This document primarily:
choices: Prevents any testing from being performed
Authorizes billing decisions
States the patient's treatment wishes and who may decide if the patient cannot
Replaces the need for identification checks
why: An advance directive documents the patient's wishes and may appoint a surrogate decision maker for when the patient loses capacity. It does not prohibit routine diagnostic testing that the patient or proxy accepts.

q: After running the tracing, the patient asks, Is my heart okay? The technician should say:
choices: I am not permitted to interpret this. Your provider will review it and discuss the results with you, usually shortly.
It looks normal to me
There is something abnormal here but I cannot say what
You should ask for a cardiology consult
why: Interpreting or hinting at findings is outside the EKG technician's scope of practice; deferring to the provider is correct. Saying it looks normal is an interpretation and can cause harm if the tracing is later read as abnormal.

q: Which task is clearly OUTSIDE the EKG technician's scope of practice?
choices: Placing precordial electrodes
Measuring the heart rate on the tracing
Adjusting the patient's beta blocker dose because the rate is 48
Reporting an abnormal rhythm to the nurse
why: Medication adjustment is a prescriber function and never delegated to a technician. Measuring rate is a technical skill and reporting findings up the chain is expected.

q: A tracing shows a wide-complex regular rhythm at 180 beats per minute in a patient complaining of dizziness. The technician should:
choices: Repeat the tracing twice before telling anyone
Notify the nurse or physician immediately and stay with the patient
Finish the rest of the department's scheduled EKGs first
Place the tracing in the chart for morning rounds
why: Ventricular tachycardia in a symptomatic patient is life threatening and requires immediate notification while monitoring the patient. Repeating the tracing first wastes time during a potentially unstable rhythm.

q: Which set of findings all require immediate escalation rather than routine charting?
choices: Ventricular fibrillation, asystole, third-degree AV block, and ST-segment elevation
Sinus arrhythmia, wandering baseline, PACs, and sinus bradycardia at 58
First-degree AV block, sinus tachycardia at 104, and an isolated PVC
Left axis deviation, low voltage, and early transition
why: These four represent arrest rhythms, complete heart block, and acute infarction, each demanding immediate provider notification. Sinus arrhythmia and isolated PACs are common and are handled in routine reporting.

q: The technician reports a critical tracing to the nurse, who does not act. The correct next step is:
choices: Tell the patient to call the doctor
Document that the nurse was told and take no further action
Post the concern in the unit group chat
Escalate up the chain of command to the charge nurse or supervisor
why: Chain of command means advancing the concern to the next level of authority when patient safety is unresolved. Documenting alone leaves a critical finding unaddressed, which is patient abandonment of responsibility.

q: Which information is required on every EKG tracing?
choices: The patient's insurance carrier
Patient name, identification number, date, time, and the technician's initials
The referring clinic's fax number
The patient's home address
why: Identification, timing, and the person who performed the test are mandatory for legal and clinical traceability. Insurance data belongs in the billing record, not on the tracing.

q: A patient must be tested sitting upright because of severe shortness of breath. The technician should:
choices: Note on the tracing that it was obtained in an upright sitting position
Record it without comment since the leads were placed correctly
Cancel the test until the patient can lie flat
Change the standardization to 5 mm/mV
why: Any deviation from the standard supine position must be documented because position alters axis and amplitude and affects comparison to prior tracings. Omitting the note risks a false interpretation of change.

q: The technician typed the wrong date into an electronic health record entry. The correct correction method is:
choices: Delete the entry and re-enter it silently
Ask IT to purge the record
Use the system's amendment function so the original entry, the correction, the author, and the time all remain visible
Overwrite the field and tell the nurse
why: Legal health records require an audit trail; corrections are made as tracked amendments that never erase the original. Deleting an entry destroys evidence and can be construed as falsification.

q: A patient slips off the step of the treadmill but is uninjured. The technician must:
choices: Say nothing since no injury occurred
Write it on the tracing only
Tell the next shift verbally
Complete an incident or occurrence report per facility policy
why: Incident reports are required for any unexpected event involving a patient, injury or not, and support risk management review. A verbal handoff leaves no formal record and does not satisfy policy.

q: The single most effective action to prevent transmission of infection between EKG patients is:
choices: Performing hand hygiene before and after every patient contact
Wearing a gown for all patients
Using a new EKG cable for each patient
Wearing gloves continuously through the shift
why: Hand hygiene remains the most effective single measure against health care associated infection. Wearing the same gloves all shift actually spreads organisms because the gloves become contaminated surfaces.

q: Standard precautions are applied to:
choices: Only patients with a known infection
Only patients on isolation
Only patients with visible wounds
Every patient, regardless of diagnosis or presumed infection status
why: Standard precautions assume all blood and body fluids may be infectious and apply universally. Limiting them to known infections fails because many carriers are undiagnosed.

q: Reusable limb electrodes and lead wires between patients should be:
choices: Rinsed with tap water
Cleaned of gel and disinfected with an approved hospital-grade disinfectant per manufacturer instructions
Wiped with alcohol only when visibly soiled
Sprayed with air freshener
why: Residual gel and skin cells harbor organisms, so mechanical cleaning followed by an EPA-registered hospital-grade disinfectant is required. Cleaning only when visibly soiled misses invisible contamination.

q: A patient is on contact precautions for Clostridioides difficile. The technician should:
choices: Use alcohol-based hand rub after removing gloves
Skip the EKG until precautions are lifted
Wear gown and gloves, and wash hands with soap and water after glove removal
Wear an N95 respirator
why: C. difficile spores resist alcohol, so soap-and-water handwashing plus gown and gloves is required. An N95 is for airborne pathogens and offers no benefit against a spore spread by contact.

q: A patient is on airborne precautions for suspected tuberculosis. Before entering with the EKG machine, the technician should:
choices: Wear a surgical mask
Leave the door open for ventilation
Bring extra staff to speed the test
Don a fit-tested N95 respirator and keep the door closed
why: Airborne precautions require a fit-tested N95 or higher and a closed negative-pressure room. A surgical mask does not filter droplet nuclei small enough to remain suspended.

q: When a portable EKG machine must be taken into an isolation room, best practice is:
choices: Take the machine in and return it to the hallway without cleaning if it did not touch the patient
Never allow the machine in the room at all
Take in only what is needed and disinfect all surfaces and cables before removing it from the room
Cover the machine with a sheet and skip disinfection
why: Equipment leaving an isolation room must be disinfected because ambient contamination reaches surfaces even without direct patient contact. A sheet cover is not a substitute for disinfection of the device.

q: Which sequence correctly lists links in the chain of infection?
choices: Infectious agent, reservoir, portal of exit, mode of transmission, portal of entry, susceptible host
Susceptible host, agent, disinfectant, reservoir, exit
Portal of entry, agent, gloves, reservoir, host
Reservoir, vaccine, host, exit, transmission
why: The six links are agent, reservoir, portal of exit, mode of transmission, portal of entry, and susceptible host. Gloves and vaccines are interventions that break links, not links themselves.

q: Hand hygiene breaks which link in the chain of infection most directly?
choices: Infectious agent
Mode of transmission
Susceptible host
Reservoir
why: Hands are the principal vehicle for indirect contact transmission, so hygiene interrupts the mode of transmission. Immunization, not hand hygiene, is what protects the susceptible host link.

q: Medical asepsis differs from surgical asepsis in that medical asepsis:
choices: Requires sterile gloves for all contact
Eliminates all spores from the skin
Reduces the number of pathogens rather than eliminating all microorganisms
Is used only in operating rooms
why: Medical asepsis, or clean technique, lowers pathogen counts and is appropriate for EKG work. Surgical asepsis eliminates all microorganisms including spores and is used for invasive procedures.

q: The OSHA Bloodborne Pathogen Standard requires employers to:
choices: Charge employees for protective equipment
Provide hepatitis B vaccination at no cost to employees with occupational exposure risk
Require all employees to donate blood annually
Test all patients for HIV before an EKG
why: The standard mandates employer-provided, no-cost hepatitis B vaccine plus an exposure control plan, PPE, and training. Mandatory patient HIV testing is not part of the standard and would violate patient rights.

q: A patient with a draining chest wound needs a 12-lead. The minimum appropriate PPE for the technician is:
choices: No PPE, hand hygiene only
N95 and face shield
Sterile gown and sterile gloves
Gloves, with a gown if splashing or soiling of clothing is anticipated
why: PPE selection is based on the anticipated exposure; gloves protect the hands and a gown is added when contamination of clothing is likely. Sterile attire is unnecessary because an EKG is not a sterile procedure.

q: A technician's ungloved hand is splashed with blood while assisting in a code. The first action is:
choices: Wash the area immediately with soap and running water
Apply bleach to the skin
Finish the code, then go home and shower
Report to the supervisor before washing
why: Immediate washing of exposed skin with soap and water is the first step, followed by prompt reporting and post-exposure evaluation. Bleach or other caustic agents damage skin and are not recommended.

q: After a needlestick from a contaminated device, reporting to employee health promptly matters most because:
choices: The device must be returned to the manufacturer
Post-exposure prophylaxis is time sensitive and most effective when started quickly
The incident report has a 30-day window
The employee must be reassigned
why: Timely evaluation allows source testing and prophylaxis, which loses effectiveness as hours pass. A long filing window does not change the clinical urgency of prophylaxis.

q: Before using an EKG machine, the technician notices a lead cable with cracked insulation and exposed wire. The correct action is:
choices: Wrap the spot in cloth tape and use it
Use it only for limb leads
Remove the machine from service, tag it, and report it for repair
Use it and note poor quality on the tracing
why: Damaged cords and cables pose shock and fire risk and must be taken out of service and tagged for biomedical repair. Taping is not an approved repair and leaves the hazard in place.

q: Proper electrical grounding of an EKG machine primarily protects against:
choices: Stray current reaching the patient and causing microshock
Wandering baseline artifact
Muscle tremor artifact
Paper jams
why: A three-prong grounded plug diverts stray current safely, preventing microshock in a patient connected to conductive electrodes. Wandering baseline is caused by respiration or loose electrodes, not grounding.

q: A patient on 4 liters of oxygen by nasal cannula is having an EKG when a small fire starts in a wastebasket. The technician should first:
choices: Open the window
Look for the fire extinguisher
Pull the alarm and then find the patient's chart
Rescue the patient by moving them away from immediate danger
why: RACE puts Rescue first, especially with oxygen present, which accelerates combustion. Searching for an extinguisher before moving the patient delays removal from a rapidly worsening hazard.

q: The P in the PASS acronym for fire extinguisher use stands for:
choices: Push the handle
Point at the flames
Prepare the area
Pull the pin
why: PASS is Pull the pin, Aim at the base of the fire, Squeeze the handle, and Sweep side to side. Aiming at the flames rather than the base fails to reach the fuel source.

q: When lifting a portable EKG machine from a low shelf, correct body mechanics require:
choices: Bending at the waist and lifting with a straight back
Bending the knees, keeping the load close to the body, and lifting with the legs
Twisting while lifting to save a step
Holding the load at arm's length for balance
why: Using the large leg muscles with the load close to the center of gravity minimizes lumbar strain. Twisting during a lift is a classic mechanism of back injury.

q: After completing a bedside EKG on an elderly patient, the technician should:
choices: Lower the bed to its lowest position and ensure the call light is within reach
Raise the bed for easier nursing access
Leave all four side rails down
Leave the bedside table pushed against the far wall
why: A low bed plus an accessible call light are core fall-prevention measures at the end of any bedside procedure. Raising the bed increases fall height and injury severity.

q: Which use of side rails is appropriate?
choices: Raising all four rails on a confused patient to keep them in bed
Removing all rails from every bed
Raising two upper rails as a mobility aid per facility policy and the care plan
Using rails instead of a bed alarm for any fall-risk patient
why: Partial rails used as an aid to repositioning are acceptable when the care plan supports it. Four raised rails on a confused patient function as a restraint and increase entrapment and climbing-over injury risk.

q: A patient collapses in the hallway, is unresponsive, and has no normal breathing and no pulse after a 10-second check. The technician should:
choices: Give two rescue breaths and wait for the code team
Check a blood pressure first
Activate the emergency response system, call for an AED, and begin chest compressions
Run a 12-lead before starting anything else
why: Unresponsive plus no breathing and no pulse is cardiac arrest, so activate the code, get the AED, and start compressions immediately. Obtaining a blood pressure or a 12-lead delays compressions and worsens survival.

q: Correct adult chest compressions are performed at:
choices: 100 to 120 per minute at a depth of 2 to 2.4 inches
60 to 80 per minute at a depth of 1 inch
140 to 160 per minute at a depth of 3 inches
80 to 100 per minute at a depth of 0.5 inch
why: Current guidelines specify a rate of 100 to 120 compressions per minute and a depth of 2 to 2.4 inches in adults. Slower or shallower compressions generate inadequate coronary perfusion pressure.

q: For adult AED use, the pads are placed:
choices: Both pads over the sternum
One over each nipple
Both pads on the back
Upper right chest below the clavicle and lower left chest at the midaxillary line
why: Anterolateral placement puts the heart in the current path between the pads. Placing both pads on the sternum leaves the myocardium outside the shock vector.

q: A patient in the waiting room grabs his throat and cannot speak, cough, or breathe. The technician should:
choices: Give a drink of water
Deliver abdominal thrusts and call for help
Perform a blind finger sweep first
Place the patient supine and start compressions
why: A conscious adult with complete airway obstruction needs abdominal thrusts while help is summoned. A blind finger sweep can push the object deeper and is not recommended.

q: During a treadmill stress test the patient becomes pale, diaphoretic, and says the room is spinning. The technician should first:
choices: Stop the test, assist the patient to a safe sitting or lying position, and alert the supervising provider
Increase the grade to finish the stage
Tell the patient to keep walking and look forward
Leave to find the physician
why: Presyncope is a termination indicator; stopping and protecting the patient from a fall comes before anything else, with immediate provider notification. Leaving the patient alone risks an unwitnessed collapse.

q: Blood returning from the body enters the heart first at the:
choices: Left atrium
Right ventricle
Right atrium
Left ventricle
why: Systemic venous blood enters the right atrium via the superior and inferior vena cavae. The left atrium receives oxygenated blood from the pulmonary veins, which is later in the circuit.

q: The valve between the left atrium and the left ventricle is the:
choices: Tricuspid valve
Mitral valve
Pulmonic valve
Aortic valve
why: The mitral, or bicuspid, valve is the left atrioventricular valve. The tricuspid is the right-sided atrioventricular valve and is easily confused with it.

q: The left anterior descending artery chiefly supplies the:
choices: SA node in most people
Posterior right atrium
Lateral wall only
Anterior wall of the left ventricle and most of the interventricular septum
why: The LAD perfuses the anterior LV wall and the anterior two thirds of the septum, so its occlusion produces anterior ST elevation in V1 through V4. The SA node is supplied by the right coronary artery in most people.

q: The intrinsic rate of the SA node in a healthy adult is:
choices: 20 to 40 beats per minute
40 to 60 beats per minute
60 to 100 beats per minute
100 to 150 beats per minute
why: The SA node fires at 60 to 100 per minute and is the normal pacemaker. The 40 to 60 range belongs to the AV junction, which takes over only if the SA node fails.

q: If the SA node fails entirely and the AV junction takes over, the expected rate is:
choices: 100 to 120 per minute
80 to 100 per minute
20 to 40 per minute
40 to 60 per minute
why: The AV junctional escape rate is 40 to 60 per minute. A rate of 20 to 40 indicates a ventricular or Purkinje escape focus, the next backup down.

q: A ventricular escape rhythm originating in the Purkinje fibers typically occurs at:
choices: 20 to 40 beats per minute
40 to 60 beats per minute
60 to 100 beats per minute
110 to 130 beats per minute
why: Purkinje and ventricular pacemakers fire at 20 to 40 per minute, the slowest escape level. The 40 to 60 range is junctional, not ventricular.

q: Ventricular diastole is the phase in which the ventricles:
choices: Contract and eject blood
Relax and fill with blood
Depolarize producing the QRS
Close the atrioventricular valves
why: Diastole is relaxation and filling; systole is contraction and ejection. The QRS marks ventricular depolarization, which initiates systole rather than diastole.

q: Cardiac output is calculated as:
choices: Heart rate divided by stroke volume
Blood pressure times heart rate
Stroke volume divided by ejection fraction
Stroke volume multiplied by heart rate
why: Cardiac output equals stroke volume times heart rate, normally about 4 to 8 liters per minute in adults. Multiplying blood pressure by heart rate gives the rate pressure product, a workload index, not output.

q: A patient takes metoprolol, a beta blocker. The expected EKG-related effect is:
choices: A slower heart rate and possible prolonged PR interval
A faster heart rate
Widened QRS complexes
Tall peaked T waves
why: Beta blockers slow SA node firing and AV conduction, producing bradycardia and sometimes first-degree block. Tachycardia is the opposite of their pharmacologic action.

q: Which medication is classically associated with a scooped or sagging ST segment sometimes called the dig effect?
choices: Furosemide
Digoxin
Nitroglycerin
Aspirin
why: Digoxin produces the characteristic scooped ST depression at therapeutic levels, which is an effect rather than ischemia. Furosemide affects the tracing indirectly through potassium loss, not by a signature ST shape.

q: Amiodarone is best classified as a:
choices: Diuretic
Beta agonist
Antiarrhythmic that can prolong the QT interval
Vasodilator used for angina
why: Amiodarone is an antiarrhythmic that prolongs repolarization and therefore the QT interval. Nitroglycerin, not amiodarone, is the vasodilator used for angina.

q: A patient reports taking sublingual nitroglycerin for chest pain. Its principal action is to:
choices: Increase heart rate directly
Thin the blood
Dilate vessels, reducing cardiac workload and relieving anginal pain
Block potassium channels
why: Nitroglycerin is a vasodilator that lowers preload and myocardial oxygen demand, relieving angina. Blood thinning describes anticoagulants and antiplatelets, a different drug class.

q: A patient on long-term furosemide has a tracing with flattened T waves and prominent U waves. The most likely explanation is:
choices: Hyperkalemia
Hypokalemia from diuretic-induced potassium loss
Hypercalcemia
Digoxin toxicity alone
why: Loop diuretics waste potassium, and hypokalemia classically flattens T waves and produces U waves. Hyperkalemia instead causes tall peaked T waves, the opposite pattern.

q: Which is a NON-modifiable risk factor for coronary artery disease?
choices: Cigarette smoking
Sedentary lifestyle
Family history of premature coronary disease
Untreated hypertension
why: Age, sex, ethnicity, and family history cannot be changed. Smoking, inactivity, and treated blood pressure are all modifiable through behavior or therapy.

q: Which group of risk factors is entirely modifiable?
choices: Age, sex, and heredity
Race, age, and family history
Sex, heredity, and diabetes type 1
Smoking, obesity, physical inactivity, and elevated LDL cholesterol
why: All four in the correct choice respond to behavior change or treatment. Age, sex, and heredity are fixed characteristics and cannot be altered.

q: A 62-year-old woman with diabetes reports two days of unusual fatigue, nausea, and jaw discomfort but denies chest pain. The technician should recognize this as:
choices: Clearly noncardiac since there is no chest pain
A possible atypical presentation of myocardial infarction warranting prompt reporting
Simple indigestion
Anxiety only
why: Women and patients with diabetes frequently present with fatigue, nausea, dyspnea, or jaw and back pain instead of classic chest pressure, partly due to neuropathy. Dismissing it because chest pain is absent is a well-documented cause of missed infarction.

q: Which is the classic description of ischemic chest pain in a typical presentation?
choices: Sharp pain that worsens with a single fingertip press
Substernal pressure or heaviness that may radiate to the left arm, jaw, or back
Pain only when swallowing
Burning pain relieved instantly by position change
why: Ischemic pain is usually a diffuse substernal pressure with radiation and associated diaphoresis or dyspnea. Pain reproduced by fingertip pressure is more suggestive of a chest wall cause.

q: Normal adult resting respiratory rate is:
choices: 12 to 20 breaths per minute
6 to 10 breaths per minute
24 to 32 breaths per minute
30 to 40 breaths per minute
why: Adult resting respirations are 12 to 20 per minute. The 30 to 40 range is normal for a newborn, not an adult.

q: A blood pressure of 148/94 mmHg in an adult is best described as:
choices: Normal
Hypotensive
Normal for an athlete
Elevated above the normal adult range and should be reported
why: Normal adult blood pressure is below about 120/80 mmHg, so 148/94 is elevated and should be reported per policy. Athletic conditioning tends to lower, not raise, resting pressure.

q: The abbreviation NPO on a cardiac order means:
choices: No pulse obtained
Nothing by mouth
Normal pacemaker output
New patient orders
why: NPO is from the Latin nil per os, meaning nothing by mouth, often ordered before stress testing or sedation. It has no relationship to pacemaker settings.

q: In the term bradycardia, the prefix brady- means:
choices: Fast
Irregular
Slow
Absent
why: Brady- means slow, so bradycardia is a slow heart rate below 60 per minute. Tachy- is the prefix meaning fast.

q: The medical root cardi- combined with the suffix -megaly means:
choices: Inflammation of the heart lining
Enlargement of the heart
Surgical repair of a valve
Study of the heart
why: The suffix -megaly means enlargement, so cardiomegaly is an enlarged heart. Inflammation would use -itis, as in carditis.

q: An equipment maintenance log for an EKG machine is kept primarily to:
choices: Track billing per test
Record patient complaints
Document calibration, service, and safety checks for quality improvement and regulatory review
Schedule technician shifts
why: Maintenance logs document that the device was verified accurate and safe, which surveyors and quality programs require. Billing and staffing are tracked in separate administrative systems.

q: The technician opens a pack of disposable electrodes and finds the expiration date passed two months ago. The correct action is:
choices: Use them if the gel still feels moist
Use them only for limb leads
Add extra gel and use them
Discard the pack, document it, and obtain unexpired electrodes
why: Expired electrodes have dried or degraded conductive gel, which produces artifact and poor signal quality, so they are removed from stock. Adding gel does not restore the validated adhesive and conductive properties.

q: A good practice for departmental supply inventory is to:
choices: Rotate stock so the oldest unexpired items are used first and restock before running out
Order only when the last box is opened
Store electrodes near a heat vent to keep gel soft
Keep all supplies in one locked office
why: First in, first out rotation with par-level restocking prevents both expiration waste and stock-outs. Heat accelerates gel drying and shortens electrode usable life.

q: Used disposable electrodes with dried gel and no visible blood should be:
choices: Placed in the sharps container
Discarded in the regular waste per facility policy
Rinsed and reused on the same patient
Placed in red biohazard bags in all cases
why: Items not saturated with blood or other potentially infectious material go in regular waste, and overuse of red bag waste is costly and unnecessary. Sharps containers are reserved for needles and other sharp items.

q: Six inpatient EKGs are ordered at once, including a STAT order on a patient with new chest pain. Best time management is to:
choices: Work in room number order
Do the fastest patients first
Perform the STAT chest pain study first, then complete the routine studies
Wait until the nurse calls again
why: STAT orders on symptomatic patients take priority because the result changes immediate treatment. Room-number sequencing ignores clinical urgency.

q: The technician cannot obtain a clean V4 because of an obese habitus and repeated artifact. The most professional action is:
choices: Ask a senior technician or supervisor for assistance and reposition carefully
Submit the tracing with artifact and no comment
Tell the patient to lose weight
Omit V4 and label the tracing as a 12-lead
why: Asking for help protects the quality of the study and is expected teamwork, not a weakness. Omitting a lead while labeling the study a 12-lead falsifies the record.

q: A coworker asks the technician to look up a neighbor's EKG results out of curiosity. The correct response is:
choices: Look it up but do not print it
Look it up if the neighbor is a friend
Ask the charge nurse to look it up instead
Refuse, because accessing records without a treatment or job-related need violates HIPAA
why: Access must be tied to a legitimate work purpose; curiosity-based lookups are auditable violations that lead to termination. Having someone else pull the record is the same violation by proxy.

q: During a bedside EKG the patient says, I am scared I am going to die. The most therapeutic response is:
choices: Do not talk like that
You sound frightened. Can you tell me more about what you are feeling?
Everyone here says that
Let me finish this tracing and then we can talk
why: Reflecting the emotion and inviting elaboration is therapeutic communication that keeps the conversation open. False reassurance or deferral shuts the patient down and misses information the care team needs.

q: Which finding on a tracing would MOST urgently require the technician to summon help before leaving the bedside?
choices: A wandering baseline
Sinus arrhythmia
A chaotic waveform with no identifiable QRS in an unresponsive patient
Occasional PACs
why: A chaotic undulating tracing without QRS complexes in an unresponsive patient indicates ventricular fibrillation, an arrest rhythm requiring immediate code activation and CPR. A wandering baseline is artifact and is corrected by improving electrode contact.

q: The technician notices a tracing showing P waves marching independently of the QRS complexes at a ventricular rate of 34. This pattern should be handled by:
choices: Filing it with the routine batch
Reporting it to the provider immediately as possible third-degree AV block
Re-running it three times before notifying anyone
Telling the patient he has heart block
why: AV dissociation with a slow ventricular escape suggests complete heart block, which is unstable and demands immediate notification. Telling the patient the diagnosis is outside the technician's scope.

q: A patient scheduled for a stress test asks whether he can skip the consent form since the doctor already explained it. The technician should:
choices: Have him sign later after the test
Sign it on his behalf to save time
Proceed without it since the explanation was given
Ensure the signed consent is completed and on the chart before the test begins
why: Informed consent must be documented and present before an invasive or higher-risk procedure such as exercise testing begins. Signing for a patient is forgery and is never acceptable regardless of intent.

q: A technician assisting a weak patient from wheelchair to exam table should:
choices: Lift the patient alone using the arms
Lock the wheelchair wheels, use a gait belt, and get assistance as needed
Pull the patient forward by the gown
Have the patient stand unaided while the technician gets the machine
why: Locking the wheels and using a gait belt with adequate help prevents both patient falls and technician injury. Leaving a weak patient to stand unassisted is a common cause of witnessed falls.
